design_detail: Comparative risk assessment, following the WHO Comparative Risk Assessment (CRA) methods of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2000 study, estimating deaths and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) attributable to alcohol in 2004 by sex, seven age groups and 14 WHO subregions (results shown for six WHO regions), with profiles of ten populous countries, plus a separate literature review of national cost-of-illness studies of which six were compared. Inputs: recorded and unrecorded adult per-capita consumption for 2003 (WHO Global Status Report on Alcohol 2004 and the WHO Global Information System on Alcohol and Health); survey-based prevalence of abstention and volume categories rescaled to per-capita consumption; drinking patterns for ischaemic heart disease and injuries; alcohol-attributable fractions taken from the CRA for 2002 (chronic diseases) and the CRA 2000 (injuries); WHO GBD 2004 deaths and DALYs for 136 causes; a new review of alcohol-use-disorder prevalence (37 studies). Counterfactual: no alcohol consumption; burden reported both as detrimental and as net of modelled protective effects. First of three papers in the Lancet Series on alcohol and global health. Design 'modelling' as the round brief directs for attributable-burden estimates: no risk-of-bias instrument applies, so the card states the design's limits with the editors' checklist (METHODS §5.3).
can_establish: Model estimates, under the WHO CRA assumptions and the stated inputs, of how many deaths and DALYs in 2004 were attributable to alcohol, globally and by sex, region, broad cause and ten countries, net of and before modelled protective effects; adult per-capita consumption by region in 2003; modelled one-year prevalence of alcohol-use disorders; and the costs reported by six national cost-of-illness studies on a common currency.
cannot_establish: Causal effects of alcohol beyond what the observational relative risks behind the attributable fractions support; how uncertain the estimates are (no uncertainty intervals are reported); the burden at any particular drinking level (the volume categories and relative risks are not given); trends since 2000 (methods and inputs changed between the 2000 and 2004 estimates); that poor or marginalised people suffer more harm per unit of alcohol (no within-population analysis); or economic costs in low-income countries (none of the six cost studies).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (modelling). Exposure: WHO Global Status Report on Alcohol 2004 and the WHO Global Information System on Alcohol and Health for 2003; recorded consumption from government taxation records, industry production and sales data and the Food and Agriculture Organization; unrecorded consumption mainly from expert opinion and general population surveys; abstention and volume distributions from large representative national surveys of the 2000s (Indicators of alcohol consumption, mortality, and burden of disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, pp. 2224–2225). Deaths and DALYs: WHO GBD 2004 update; population: United Nations 2006 revision (p. 2225). Cost studies: search of Ovid Medline, PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, PsychINFO, Google Scholar and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, January 1992 to September 2007, with hand-searching of journal content pages and citations (Panel, 1st paragraph, p. 2228).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Alcohol-use-disorder review: studies done after 1990 using ICD-10, DSM-IIIR or DSM-IV criteria for alcohol dependence and the CIDI, SCAN or AUDADIS-ADR interview (p. 2225). Causes: categories meeting standard epidemiological criteria for a causal role (consistent association, chance, confounding and bias ruled out with reasonable confidence, plausible mechanism, with most weight on temporality, consistency, biological evidence and strength of association); the same as in the CRA 2000 plus colorectal cancer after the 2007 IARC assessment; infectious diseases not included (pp. 2226, 2231). Cost studies: of 29 studies from 18 countries and the European Union, only those estimating gross cost with a 6% discount rate (5% for South Korea), the most recent and comprehensive per country: France, the USA, Scotland and Canada (high income), South Korea and Thailand (middle income) (Panel, 3rd paragraph, p. 2228).
sample.demographics: Global population in 2004 by sex and age groups 0–4, 5–14, 15–29, 30–44, 45–59, 60–69 and 70 years and older, in 14 WHO subregions defined by child and adult mortality (pp. 2227–2228); country profiles for Brazil, China, Germany, India, Japan, Nigeria, Russia, South Africa, Thailand and the USA (Table 3, p. 2227).
sample.selection_effects: The relative risks come mainly from meta-analyses of middle-class cohorts in high-income countries and are assumed to apply everywhere (Conclusions, 2nd paragraph, p. 2231). Drinking patterns were estimated from nearby countries or expert opinion where surveys were insufficient, and more than a quarter of global consumption is unrecorded and estimated mainly from expert opinion (p. 2231). The cost comparison keeps 6 of 29 identified studies, four from high-income countries, two from middle-income countries and none from low-income countries; two of the six are by authors of this paper (Canada, refs 50 and 51; Thailand, ref 45).

exposure.measurement: Modelled. Adult per-capita consumption (recorded plus unrecorded) for 2003; survey-derived volume of drinking adjusted to per-capita consumption, assuming that per-capita consumption is the most valid indicator of overall consumption and that surveys give correct proportions of volume by sex and age (pp. 2224–2225). Patterns of drinking (especially heavy drinking occasions) were used in addition to average volume for ischaemic heart disease and injuries (p. 2225).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Exposure in litres of pure alcohol (100% ethanol) per adult per year (Figure 1; Findings › Exposure to alcohol, p. 2228); abstention = no drinking in the previous year (p. 2224). The average-volume categories used to compute attributable fractions, their gram thresholds and the relative risk at each are not given in this paper; 'adult' is not defined.
exposure.polysubstance: Not modelled. The authors note possible interactions between alcohol and poverty, malnutrition or hopelessness that would introduce error (Conclusions, 2nd paragraph, p. 2231).

comparison.controls: Counterfactual of no alcohol consumption, the same for detrimental and beneficial effects (Establishing risk relations, 2nd paragraph, p. 2227). The relative risks are those of each exposure category compared with no consumption in the source meta-analyses; whether those reference groups were lifetime abstainers or all non-drinkers is not stated here.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at model level; confounding and the make-up of abstainer groups in the studies behind the relative risks are not discussed in this paper.

outcomes.instruments: WHO GBD 2004 estimates of deaths and DALYs for 136 causes (p. 2225). Alcohol-related categories listed (p. 2226): perinatal disorders and low birthweight; cancers of the mouth and oropharynx, oesophagus, colon and rectum, liver and breast, and other neoplasms; diabetes; alcohol-use disorders; unipolar depression; epilepsy; hypertensive heart disease; ischaemic heart disease; haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke; cirrhosis of the liver; road traffic injuries, falls, drownings, poisonings, other unintentional injuries; self-inflicted injuries, violence and other intentional injuries. Costs: direct health care, law enforcement, other direct social costs and indirect (productivity) costs, converted to international dollars with the IMF purchasing-power-parity index and inflated to 2007 (Panel, p. 2228–2229).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors refer to general limitations of global mortality data and of DALY assumptions and weights, without quantifying them (Conclusions, 1st paragraph, p. 2231).
outcomes.operationalization: Alcohol-attributable fraction AF = Σ Pi(RRi − 1) / [Σ Pi(RRi − 1) + 1], with Pi the prevalence of exposure category i and RRi its relative risk against no consumption (pp. 2226–2227); conditions defined by alcohol (alcohol-use disorders, alcoholic liver disease, alcohol-induced pancreatitis) are wholly attributable. Net burden = detrimental minus prevented deaths or DALYs. Alcohol-use-disorder burden from prevalence, remission (0·175 a year), relative risk of death (1·80 men, 3·84 women) and disability weights of 0·122–0·137 (pp. 2225–2226). Costs are gross: only costs of harm were counted, with no offset for any benefit (Panel, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs, p. 2228).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: estimation, no statistical tests. 25 counts the alcohol-related cause categories listed on p. 2226.

analysis.effect_sizes: No uncertainty intervals are given for any estimate. Deaths in 2004 (Table 1, p. 2224; thousands): detrimental 2482 (men 2039, women 443), prevented 227 (cardiovascular 215, diabetes 12), net 2255 of 58,738 deaths, 3·8% (men 6·3%, women 1·1%; CRA 2000 3·2%). Detrimental deaths by cause: unintentional injuries 666, cardiovascular 545, cancer 487, cirrhosis 373, intentional injuries 272, neuropsychiatric 135, perinatal 3. DALYs (Table 2, p. 2225; thousands): detrimental 73,231, prevented 2321, net 70,910 of 1,530,168, 4·6% (men 7·6%, women 1·4%; CRA 2000 4·0%); neuropsychiatric 26,682, unintentional injuries 18,604. Younger than 60: 5·3% of deaths (7·9% men, 1·9% women) (p. 2229). Regional share of deaths, both sexes: 0·5% eastern Mediterranean to 6·5% Europe; men in Europe 11·0% (Figure 2, p. 2225). One-year prevalence of alcohol-use disorders at 15–64 years: 3·6% globally (men 6·3%, women 0·9%), 10·9% in the eastern European subregion (Figure 4, p. 2226). Costs: I$122 (Thailand) to I$837 (USA) per head; 1·3% (Thailand) to 3·3% (South Korea) of GDP at purchasing-power parity (Table 4, p. 2230). Editors' calculation: detrimental deaths are 4·2% and detrimental DALYs 4·8% of the totals; cirrhosis is 15·0% of detrimental alcohol-attributable deaths.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable. Attributable fractions are computed by sex, age group and region; patterns of drinking enter for ischaemic heart disease and injuries.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The relative risks, volume categories, exposure prevalences and cause-specific attributable fractions that produce every estimate are not shown; they are referred to earlier CRA reports (refs 12 and 34). Results are shown for six WHO regions rather than the 14 subregions modelled. The list of the 29 cost studies is in a web appendix, not on file. No sensitivity analysis is reported.
analysis.power: Not applicable. No uncertainty analysis is reported; the conclusions cite an earlier WHO report (World Health Report 2002, ref 7) for the uncertainty of alcohol estimates being fairly low compared with other risk factors (p. 2231).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Under the WHO CRA assumptions, alcohol was estimated to account for 2·48 million deaths in 2004 before and 2·26 million after subtracting 0·23 million deaths it was modelled to prevent (3·8% of all deaths), and for 4·6% of net DALYs, with the burden concentrated in men, in Europe and the Americas, and in ages 15–59. Net burden varied from 28·1% of DALYs in Russian men to a small net benefit in German women (−0·4%). Six national cost-of-illness studies put alcohol's gross costs at 1·3% to 3·3% of GDP. None of these figures carries an uncertainty interval, and no sensitivity analysis is reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that disease burden is closely related to average volume and, “for every unit of exposure, is strongest in poor people” and in people marginalised from society (p. 2223); the findings speak of alcohol-attributable mortality relative to volume being higher in developing countries, and of the proportion of alcohol-attributable deaths having increased since 2000, mainly because more women drink (pp. 2228–2229); the conclusions say the burden has not fallen since 2000 and probably increased, and that the uncertainty of the estimates is fairly low compared with other risk factors (p. 2231). Gaps: (1) the paper presents no estimate of burden per unit of alcohol by income or marginalisation, and its relative risks are the same in every population, so any per-unit difference in the model comes from modelled drinking patterns, abstention and cause-of-death structure rather than from measured vulnerability; (2) the comparison with 2000 mixes a real change with method changes (new alcohol-use-disorder prevalence and disability weights, colorectal cancer added, GBD 2004 cause revisions, attributable fractions from 2000 and 2002), so it cannot show that the burden rose or why; (3) no uncertainty is quantified in the paper; (4) that burden tracks average volume is built into the model, not found by it; (5) the abstract's cost statement uses gross national product, while the table uses GDP and the panel itself warns that expressing costs as a share of GDP poses a serious methodological problem.

timeline.event: Comparative Risk Assessment for 2000 (Rehm et al., in Ezzati et al., Comparative quantification of health risks; ref 12): 3·2% of deaths and 4·0% of DALYs attributable to alcohol, the comparison rows of Tables 1 and 2, and the source of the injury attributable fractions used here.
Comparative Risk Assessment for 2002 (Rehm et al., WHO report; ref 34), source of the chronic-disease attributable fractions used here.
IARC working group assessment of the carcinogenicity of alcoholic beverages (Baan et al., Lancet Oncol; ref 31), on which colorectal cancer was added to the causes.

This paper, first of three in the Lancet Series on alcohol and global health; the companion papers are Anderson, Chisholm and Fuhr (2009) on the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of alcohol policies and Casswell and Thamarangsi (2009), a call to action. The same issue carried an editorial (p. 2171), three comments (pp. 2173, 2174, 2176) and a perspective (p. 2191), which were not read.

Rehm et al. cirrhosis meta-analysis cites this paper for about 15% of alcohol-attributable deaths in 2004 being due to cirrhosis (Table 1 here: 373 of 2482 thousand detrimental deaths) and was done to supply cirrhosis relative risks to the GBD 2005 CRA (card sc_rehm_2010).

GBD 2016 alcohol analysis (Griswold et al.), with new relative-risk curves for 23 outcomes and an estimated theoretical minimum of zero drinks: 2·8 million attributable deaths in 2016 (card sc_griswold_2018, this round); the GBD 2020 analysis (Bryazka et al., 2022) revised it again (card sc_bryazka_2022).

replication.where_it_stands: A dated estimate (2004 deaths, 2003 exposure, attributable fractions from the 2000 and 2002 CRAs) built on the WHO CRA alcohol estimates for 2000 and 2002, whose support went to the first author. Later GBD rounds changed the relative-risk curves, the treatment of protective effects and the counterfactual (sc_griswold_2018), so its numbers should be cited only as 2004 WHO-CRA estimates, with their assumptions, and not compared directly with later estimates. Its cost comparison rests on six national studies from 1997 to 2006.

funding.funder: The comparative risk assessments for alcohol for 2000 and 2002 underlying the study were supported by WHO and the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health to the first author; the specific work for this paper by the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto (Acknowledgments, p. 2231).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (p. 2231).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and the University of Toronto, the WHO Collaboration Centre for Substance Abuse (Zurich), TU Dresden, WHO's Department of Health Statistics (Geneva), and Thailand's Health Intervention and Technology Assessment Program at the Ministry of Public Health and Mahidol University (p. 2223). The model's inputs are largely the first author's group's earlier work (CRA 2000 and 2002, the alcohol-use-disorder review, ref 24), and two of the six cost studies compared are by authors of this paper (Canada and Thailand). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A re-estimation for the same year that propagates uncertainty in recorded and unrecorded consumption, drinking patterns, relative risks and cause-specific deaths into uncertainty intervals, with sensitivity analyses on the protective cardiovascular and diabetes relative risks and on the transfer of relative risks across countries; and cost-of-illness studies done to one protocol in low- and middle-income countries.

domains.note: Recorded consumption from taxation, industry and FAO data is a sound base, but more than a quarter of global consumption is unrecorded and estimated mainly by expert opinion, drinking patterns come from nearby countries or expert opinion where surveys were lacking, cause-of-death data are of uneven quality, and the exposure behind the attributable fractions dates from the 2000 and 2002 CRAs rather than 2004; regional and country figures for places with much unrecorded drinking carry more of this.

Taken from observational meta-analyses (via the CRA 2000 and 2002) that the authors describe as based mainly on middle-class cohorts in high-income countries and assume to hold in every population; not shown in this paper; the protective relative risks for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes, which subtract 227,000 deaths, come from the low-intake range where confounding and abstainer bias are most disputed; no appraisal of the underlying studies.

No alcohol consumption, stated explicitly and applied to harms and benefits alike, and detrimental and net figures are both reported, which shows how much the protective estimates matter; but whether 'no consumption' in the source relative risks means lifetime abstention or all non-drinkers is not stated.

domains.domain: Uncertainty intervals: what they include and exclude
domains.note: No uncertainty intervals for any burden or cost estimate; the only intervals in the paper are for the relative risk of death with an alcohol-use disorder. The statement that uncertainty is fairly low rests on an earlier WHO report.
No sensitivity analysis is reported, for example to unrecorded consumption, drinking patterns, the protective relative risks or the transfer of relative risks between countries.

A described search with an explicit rule for comparability (gross cost, 6% discount rate, most recent study per country), but only six studies, none from a low-income country, from different years (1997 to 2006) and methods, two by the authors; gross costs only; population-weighted averages dominated by the USA; the list of 29 studies is in a web appendix not on file.

Tables 1 to 4 are complete and add up within rounding (editors' check), but the inputs that drive the estimates are only referenced, and several statements do not match the tables (neuropsychiatric shares, the alcohol-use-disorder age range, South Korea's income group, a net benefit in German women against the conclusion).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for burden-of-disease modelling (METHODS §5.3; the round brief sets design 'modelling' with no instrument). The editors' checklist is used with domains for the inputs, the relative-risk functions, the counterfactual, the uncertainty intervals, the sensitivity of the headline and the reporting, as in card sc_griswold_2018, with a domain added for the cost comparison; the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The estimates are transparent model outputs whose tables add up, but they carry no uncertainty and no sensitivity analysis, and their net figures rest on protective relative risks from disputed low-intake studies. Citable as the WHO-CRA estimates for 2004 (deaths, DALYs, regional and country shares, the modelled prevalence of alcohol-use disorders) and for the costs reported by six national studies, always with these assumptions; not citable for trends since 2000, for greater harm per unit of alcohol in poor or marginalised people, or for the precision of the figures.

key_findings.finding: Exposure: worldwide average consumption in 2003 was 6·2 L of pure alcohol per adult per year, highest in the WHO European region (11·9 L) and the Americas (8·7 L) and lowest in the eastern Mediterranean region (0·7 L). Most adults abstained (no drinking in the previous year): 45% of men and 66% of women. Consumption rose with GDP per adult up to about I$10 000 and abstention fell with GDP up to about $7000.
key_findings.locator: Indicators of alcohol consumption, mortality, and burden of disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2224); Findings › Exposure to alcohol, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2228); Figure 1 (p. 2224)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; Figure 1 is a map and was not used for values)

key_findings.finding: Deaths in 2004, against a counterfactual of no alcohol consumption (thousands): 2482 deaths caused (men 2039, women 443) and 227 prevented (cardiovascular 215, diabetes 12), net 2255 of 58 738 deaths, or 3·8% (men 1944, 6·3%; women 311, 1·1%); the CRA for 2000 gave 3·2%. Deaths caused, by category: unintentional injuries 666, cardiovascular 545, cancer 487, cirrhosis of the liver 373, intentional injuries 272, neuropsychiatric 135, perinatal 3.
key_findings.note: Percentages in Table 1 are shares of all deaths caused or prevented by alcohol, not attributable fractions. Editors' calculation: deaths caused are 4·2% of all deaths, and cirrhosis is 15·0% of the deaths caused (14·6% in men, 17·1% in women as printed).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Age: 5·3% of deaths under age 60 were attributable to alcohol (7·9% in men, 1·9% in women), against 3·8% at all ages, mainly through injuries; most protective effects fell in older age groups.

Net alcohol-attributable share of deaths by WHO region (both sexes): Africa 2·4%, Americas 5·6%, eastern Mediterranean 0·5%, Europe 6·5%, southeast Asia 2·3%, western Pacific 5·3%; men in Europe 11·0%, women 0·1% (eastern Mediterranean) to 1·8% (Americas, Europe).
key_findings.locator: Figure 2, printed values below the bars
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; Figure 2's printed values checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Alcohol-attributable death rates per 10 000 people younger than 70 years: men 1·1 (eastern Mediterranean) to 15·0 (Europe), women 0·2 to 3·5; global 7·4 in men and 1·4 in women, about 5·2 times higher in men, from about four-fold (Europe) to almost ten-fold (southeast Asia).

DALYs in 2004 (thousands): 73 231 caused (men 61 881, women 11 349) and 2321 prevented, net 70 910 of 1 530 168, or 4·6% (men 60 806, 7·6%; women 10 104, 1·4%); the CRA for 2000 gave 4·0%. DALYs caused, by category: neuropsychiatric 26 682, unintentional injuries 18 604, intentional injuries 7660, cirrhosis 6945, cardiovascular 6924, cancer 6268.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: DALYs caused are 4·8% of all DALYs; neuropsychiatric conditions are 36·4% of the DALYs caused.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; Table 2 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Age profile of the burden: 33·6% of alcohol-attributable DALYs fell at ages 15–29, 31·3% at 30–44 and 22·0% at 45–59; in these ages alcohol accounted for more than 10% of all DALYs in men and 2–3% in women; 0·3% of DALYs at ages 0–4 and 3·7% at 70 and older.

Net alcohol-attributable share of DALYs by WHO region (both sexes): Africa 2·1%, Americas 9·2%, eastern Mediterranean 0·5%, Europe 11·6%, southeast Asia 2·7%, western Pacific 7·2%, world 4·6%; men in Europe 17·3% and the Americas 14·2%.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3, printed values below the bars
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; Figure 3's printed values checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Modelled one-year prevalence of alcohol-use disorders at ages 15–64 in 2004: world 3·6% (men 6·3%, women 0·9%); highest in the eastern European subregion with high adult mortality (10·9%; men 19·2%) and lowest in the eastern Mediterranean region (0·3%). Years lived with disability for alcohol-use disorders: 22·0 million in 2004 against 19·1 million in 2000.
key_findings.locator: Figure 4, printed values (p. 2226); Findings › Alcohol-use disorders, 2nd paragraph (p. 2230)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; Figure 4's printed values checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Alcohol-use-disorder model inputs: point prevalence of alcohol dependence at ages 18–64 from 37 studies, adjusted by age and sex for harmful use and comorbidity; remission rate 0·175 a year from age 15; relative risk of death 1·80 (95% CI 1·76–1·84) in men and 3·84 (3·54–4·15) in women; disability weights lowered from 0·18 to 0·122–0·137 by combining the dependence weight with a lower weight for harmful use.

Ten countries, net alcohol-attributable share of all DALYs: men in Russia 28·1%, Brazil 17·7%, China 12·9%, Germany 12·8%, Thailand 12·1%, USA 12·1%, South Africa 7·8%, Japan 6·7%, India 4·9%, Nigeria 2·4%; women in Russia 10·7%, USA 4·5%, Brazil 3·4% and Germany −0·4% (a net benefit of 17 thousand DALYs, printed as −17). Attributable fraction of cirrhosis DALYs in men from 47% (India) to 88% (Russia), in women from 4% (India) to 82% (Russia). Protective effects appear only for Germany, Japan and the USA.
key_findings.note: In Table 3 the percentages beside each cause are attributable fractions (the share of that cause's DALYs due to alcohol), unlike Tables 1 and 2, where they are shares of all alcohol-attributable deaths or DALYs.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; Table 3 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Method of attribution: alcohol-attributable fractions combine the prevalence of each exposure category with its relative risk against no consumption from meta-analyses; fractions for chronic diseases were taken from the CRA for 2002 and for injuries from the CRA 2000, and take account of drinking patterns for ischaemic heart disease and injuries; the counterfactual of no alcohol consumption is the same for harms and benefits.

Economic costs (2007 international dollars at purchasing-power parity, gross costs, 6% discount rate except 5% for South Korea): cost per head I$358 (Scotland), I$384 (France), I$420 (Canada) and I$837 (USA) in high-income countries, I$524 (South Korea) and I$122 (Thailand) in middle-income countries; total cost 1·4% (Scotland, Canada), 1·7% (France), 2·7% (USA), 3·3% (South Korea) and 1·3% (Thailand) of GDP. Indirect productivity costs were the largest component, from 49·0% of the total in Canada to 94·8% in Thailand.
key_findings.note: The weighted-average columns are population-weighted means of the countries' figures (editors' check), so the high-income average is dominated by the USA; they are not totals for any population.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; Table 4 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Cost-study selection: the search found 247 abstracts and 45 full-text reports; 29 studies from 18 countries and the European Union reported cost data; because methods differed (net against gross costs; discount rates from 3% to 10%), only six methodologically comparable studies were compared.
key_findings.locator: Panel (Economic costs attributable to alcohol), 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; web appendix with the 29 studies not on file)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: more than 25% of global consumption is unrecorded and estimated mainly from expert opinion; drinking patterns had to be estimated from nearby countries or expert opinion; relative risks from meta-analyses mainly of middle-class cohorts in developed countries were assumed to transfer to all countries; alcohol-attributable infectious diseases such as tuberculosis and pneumonia were not included.

The authors' reading of protective effects: a net cardiovascular benefit may exist only in regions where alcohol is drunk regularly and lightly without heavy drinking occasions, and only in older people; elsewhere the net cardiovascular effect is detrimental; globally they put the burden from alcohol at about the size of that from smoking in 2000.

Cancer categories counted as alcohol-related (ICD-10): mouth and oropharynx (C00–C14), oesophagus (C15), colon and rectum (C18–C21), liver (C22), breast (C50) and other neoplasms (D00–D48); the same as in the CRA 2000 except colorectal cancer, added after the 2007 IARC assessment. The 487 thousand cancer deaths of Table 1 are not broken down by site.
key_findings.locator: Identification of disease categories causally linked to alcohol, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The oesophageal and liver categories are whole-organ codes (all histological types), unlike later models that count only squamous cell oesophageal and hepatocellular liver cancer (card sc_rumgay_2021).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 36·4% of all neuropsychiatric DALYs and 5·4% of all neuropsychiatric deaths were caused by alcohol (p. 2229). In Tables 1 and 2 these are the neuropsychiatric shares of the deaths and DALYs caused by alcohol, not alcohol's share of all neuropsychiatric deaths and DALYs (editors' calculation: 26,682 of 73,231 thousand DALYs and 135 of 2482 thousand deaths).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence misstates the denominator; alcohol's attributable fraction of all neuropsychiatric burden cannot be taken from it, and claims should not cite it.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; Tables 1 and 2 checked on the rendered pages)

reporting_issues.issue: The exposure data are described for 2003 (p. 2224), but the attributable fractions applied to 2004 deaths were taken from the CRA for 2002 (chronic diseases) and the CRA 2000 (injuries) (p. 2227); yet the findings attribute the rise from 3·2% to 3·8% since 2000 mainly to more women drinking (p. 2229).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which year's drinking the 2004 estimates reflect is unclear, and the change since 2000 also reflects changed methods and inputs (alcohol-use-disorder prevalence and weights, colorectal cancer, the GBD 2004 cause revision); it cannot be read as a measured trend.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods take the point prevalence of alcohol dependence at ages 18–64 from 37 studies (p. 2225), while Figure 4 reports the one-year prevalence of all alcohol-use disorders at ages 15–64 (p. 2226); the step from one to the other is described only as an adjustment for harmful use and comorbidity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Figure 4 prevalences are model outputs extended beyond the age range and prevalence period of the data; they should be cited as modelled.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; Figure 4 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusions state that even where the net cardiovascular effect is beneficial, the overall effect of alcohol on the burden of disease is detrimental (p. 2231), but Table 3 gives German women a net benefit of 17 thousand DALYs (printed as −17) (−0·4% of all DALYs).
reporting_issues.consequence: The model itself yields a net benefit for one population; the general statement holds for regions, not for every population.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; Table 3 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: The panel's text places South Korea among the high-income countries when describing direct costs (6th paragraph, p. 2229), while Table 4 lists it as a middle-income country.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table's classification should be used.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Rehm_2009_GlobalBurdenEconomicCost.pdf (all text read; Table 4 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says costs exceed 1% of gross national product (p. 2223), whereas Table 4 reports costs as a share of GDP at purchasing-power parity, and the panel itself says that expressing these costs as a share of GDP poses a serious methodological challenge (p. 2229).
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline cost ratio uses a different aggregate from the table and a framing the authors themselves caution against; claims should quote the table's figures with the measure named.

reporting_issues.issue: No burden or cost estimate carries an uncertainty interval, while the conclusions describe the uncertainty as fairly low compared with other risk factors, citing the World Health Report 2002 (p. 2231).
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of every number on this card is unknown; claims citing it must say the figures come without uncertainty intervals.

reporting_issues.issue: The list of alcohol-related categories gives cirrhosis of the liver as K74 (p. 2226), while alcoholic liver disease (K70) is named as wholly attributable to alcohol (p. 2226); where K70 deaths are counted in Tables 1 to 3 is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the totals, but the cirrhosis figures cannot be matched to a code definition from the paper alone.
